8b5234d502.q: How did Teresa Knox start Community Care College and what was the turning point in her entrepreneurial journey?
8b5234d502.a: Teresa started her first legitimate business, a dental assistant school, in her early 20s while living on Riverside Drive in Tulsa as a single mother. She placed a $4 ad in the local paper and trained people for employment. The pivotal moment came when a woman with a nice car and job—whom she called a 'fancy lady'—asked about her program price, and Teresa quoted $1,000. The woman wrote a check, came to her apartment on Saturdays to be trained, and secured a job as a dental assistant. 'That's when that really that entrepreneurial bug was really planted in my heart,' Knox said, marking the moment she realized the power of her business model.

7c67adbd36.q: What was Clary Sage College and why did Teresa Knox create it as a separate institution?
7c67adbd36.a: Clary Sage College was a branch campus of Community Care College that Teresa Knox launched over 20 years ago after noticing her medical students were going into the medical spa industry. She interviewed 1,000 cosmetologists and visited 40-50 schools across the nation before launching programs in cosmetology, barbering, skincare, makeup artistry, fashion, and interior design—what she calls 'Blue Oceans' or uncharted business territory. The college offered these creative-oriented, short-term training programs leading to entry-level employment, distinct from Community Care College's medical and legal programs.

9b15fb5d14.q: Why did Teresa Knox convert her for-profit colleges to nonprofit status?
9b15fb5d14.a: Teresa Knox started her schools as for-profit institutions and planned to sell at their 20th anniversary to a private equity firm. However, she got 'cold feet' because it felt like 'giving up a baby for adoption.' At that time, they had not raised tuition in 10 years, were giving millions in scholarships, and were one of the last single-shareholder for-profit institutions of higher education in America. After praying that night, Knox decided to back out of the sale and convert to nonprofit status, feeling she needed God's help to know what to do with the business.

e14d33cf74.q: What role did breaking generational poverty play in Teresa Knox's mission for her colleges?
e14d33cf74.a: Teresa Knox came from a family with generational poverty, abuse, and addiction; many family members did not graduate past ninth grade and several are no longer alive. She became a dental assistant at age 15-16, which 'probably saved my life' and broke the cycle of poverty that had plagued her family for multiple generations. This experience shaped her belief that 'if you have one stable true thing in your life, like a job you can be proud of, that you're contributing to society, then anything can work out.' Her colleges were designed to provide that same pathway for students seeking viable employment outside traditional four-year degrees.

173da5e051.q: What are the top employment pathways in Oklahoma that do not require a bachelor's degree?
173da5e051.a: Teresa Knox noted that 'if you look at the top 100 jobs that Oklahoma needs to be sustainable over the next 25 years, over half do not require a bachelor's degree.' She emphasized the need for skilled trade workers and cited examples like HVAC, plumbing, and electrical work as high-demand, well-paying careers. She also highlighted that there is significant 'disruption in higher education right now' with questions about the ROI on college degrees, especially considering debt and viable alternative training pathways.
